claims.claim_text: Incumbent governments globally are entering a compressed political time horizon where voter patience has collapsed from electoral cycles to under two years, creating a structural acceleration of policy risk and regime uncertainty.
reasoning_chain: Step 1: Starmer won a historic landslide in July 2024 and resigned in under two years — Snider uses this as evidence that the traditional 4-5 year political mandate no longer provides incumbents with policy latitude.
Step 2: This compression is driven by the intensity of household economic pain — voters no longer grant leaders time to implement structural reforms when daily financial stress is acute.
Step 3: Snider extends this to the US, noting early warning signals in off-cycle elections (Virginia, New Jersey) and framing the 2026 midterms as a direct analogue to the UK dynamic.

Step 4: The result is a structurally unstable policy environment where governments cannot pursue long-term economic repair because short-term voter pressure forces reactive, often counterproductive policy responses.
Step 5: For macro investors, this means elevated policy uncertainty and a higher frequency of regime changes, which increases volatility and risk premia across asset classes.
claims.speaker_confidence_signals: Strong declarative framing ('voters are no longer patient,' 'Starmer only got two years'), specific references to US electoral calendar and named states, though the predictive extension to the US is somewhat asserted.
claims.time_horizon_detail: 12-24 months, centered on 2026 US midterm cycle
claims.novelty_note: The specific framing of political time horizon compression as a structural feature — not just a one-off — is a moderately novel analytical angle for Snider, who typically focuses on financial plumbing rather than political science. The Starmer case study gives it fresh empirical grounding.
claims.catalyst: US 2026 midterm elections; Republican policy messaging on economy in Q3-Q4 2026
